title: Ways to Split a Number Into Parts

concept.title: Count by the largest part you may still use
body: Write `n` as a sum of positive integers. The order of the parts does not matter, so `3 + 2` and `2 + 3` are the same way. To avoid counting an order twice, write the parts from the biggest to the smallest and think of the problem as `parts(n, m)`: the number of ways to write `n` with parts that are **at most `m`**.

Look at the biggest part `m`. Either at least one part is equal to `m`: take it away and write `n - m` with parts at most `m` again. Or no part is equal to `m`: write `n` with parts at most `m - 1`. The two cases never overlap and together they cover everything:
The same pair `(n, m)` is reached by many different paths, so store each answer in a table (a **memo**) the first time it is computed. With the table there are only `n * n` different states.

statement: Count the ways to write `n` as a sum of positive integers when the order of the parts does not matter (`3 + 2` and `2 + 3` are one way). The number `n` itself is also a way.
hints: Define parts(n, m) as the number of ways to write n with parts of size at most m.
Either use a part of size m (then n - m is left, with parts at most m) or do not use it (parts at most m - 1).
Without a table the same states are computed again and again: store every answer.

explanation: `parts(n, m)` is the number of ways to write `n` with parts of size at most `m`. It equals the ways that use a part `m` (`parts(n - m, m)`) plus the ways that do not (`parts(n, m - 1)`). The memo makes each of the `n * n` states cost one addition.
